patient_note_history:
History 
HPI: A 51-year-old male construction worker complains of low back pain that started after he lifted heavy boxes 1 week ago. The pain is sharp in nature, rates 8/10, and radiates to the left thigh and sometimes to the left foot. Pain worsens with movement, coughing, and sitting for a long time. It is relieved by lying down and partially by ibuprofen. He denies urinary or stool incontinence, as well as weakness or loss of sensation in the lower extremities. No fever, night sweats, or weight loss. He does report difficulty urinating and incomplete emptying of the bladder for 6 months, as well as a 1-year history of intermittent low back pain. The pain is exacerbated by sitting for long periods but is relieved by lying down after ambulation. 
ROS: Negative, except as above. 
Allergies: Penicillin (causes rash). 
Medications: Ibuprofen. 
PMH: No. 
PSH: No. 
SH: Smokes 1 pack per day for 18 years, drinks 1-2 beers on weekends, CAGE 0/4. 
FH: Noncontributory.

exam_lines.source_text: Patient is in mild distress due to back pain.
Back: Mild paraspinal muscle tenderness bilaterally. Range of motion within normal limits, no warmth or erythema.
Extremities: 2+ popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses bilaterally.
Hips: Non-tender and normal range of motion bilaterally.

Neuro: Motor strength is 5/5 throughout, including left great toe dorsiflexion. DTRs are 2+ symmetric, Babinski sign bilaterally. Gait is normal (including toe-to-heel walking), although he walks with his back slightly bent forward. Straight leg raising is 80 degrees bilaterally. Sensation is intact.

gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Lumbar muscle strain: This often follows strenuous or unusual exertion, but pain usually does not radiate to the extremities. Paraspinal muscle tenderness is often present. 
• Degenerative arthritis: Degenerative back diseases are common, and typically, pain is exacerbated by activity and alleviated by rest. Radicular symptoms may be present. 
• Multiple myeloma: Typically, patients are older than 50 years of age. Back and bone pain may be the only presenting complaint. Anemia, neuropathy, hypercalcemia, and renal failure are also common. 
• Malingering: This is defined as intentional faking of symptoms for secondary gain (e.g., getting out of work).
raw_opening:
Opening Scenario:

Rick Meyer, a 51-year-old male construction worker, comes to the office complaining of back pain.

Vital Signs:

- BP: 120/85 mmHg
- Temp: 98.2°F (36.8°C)
- RR: 20/minute
- HR: 50/minute, regular

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or felted breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Checklist/SP Sheet:

Patient Description:

Patient - a 51-year-old male who lives with his girlfriend.

Notes for the SP:

- Pretend that you have para-spinal lower back tenderness when examined.
- Show normal reflexes, sensation, and strength in both lower extremities.
- Lean forward slightly when walking.

Challenging Questions to Ask:

"I believe I am unable to attend work, doctor. Could you provide a letter for my employer to grant me some time off?"

Sample Examinee Response:

"You're right; heavy construction work can worsen your back pain or cause it to heal more slowly. To evaluate whether you require time off, I will need to ask you several questions and conduct a physical examination.."

Examinee Checklist:

Entrance:

- The examinee knocked on the door before entering.
- The examinee made eye contact with the SP.
- The examinee correctly used the patient's name.
- The examinee introduced themselves by name.
- The examinee identified their role or position.

Reflective Listening:

- The examinee asked an open-ended question and actively listened to the response.
- The examinee asked the SP to list his/her concerns and listened to the response without interrupting.
- The examinee summarized the SP's concerns, often using the SP's own words.

Information Gathering:
- The examinee dictated data efficiently and accurately.

Connecting With the Patient:
The examinee recognized the SP's emotions and responded with PEARLS.


Physical Examination:

- The examinee washed his/her hands.
- The examinee asked for permission to start the exam.
- The examinee used respectful draping.
- The examinee did not repeat painful maneuvers.

Exam Component Maneuver:

- Musculoskeletal exam (back): Inspection, palpation, range of motion
- Extremities: Inspection, palpation of peripheral pulses, hip exam
- Neurologic exam: Motor, deep tendon reflexes (DTRs), Babinski sign, gait (including toe-to-heel walking), passive straight leg raising, sensory exam

Closure:

- The examinee discussed initial diagnostic impressions.
- The examinee discussed initial management plans.
- Follow-up tests: The examinee mentioned the need for a rectal exam.
- The examinee asked if the SP had any other questions or concerns.

Sample Closure:

"Mr. Meyer, I am worried about your challenges with urination.. I would like to conduct a rectal examination to evaluate your prostate for any benign growths or cancer.. I would also like to order some blood tests, an X-ray, and possibly an MRI of your back to better determine the cause of your pain. It could be due to a pinched nerve or muscle spasm. In the meantime, I will write a note to your employer requesting that you be assigned only light duties at work and provide recommendations on proper posture for lifting heavy objects to prevent similar episodes in the future. Additionally, I strongly advise you to quit smoking and can provide a prescription for medication or nicotine replacement if needed. Do you have any questions for me?"Patient Note:
